data.title: How to check a forex broker in 5 minutes
slides: Find the legal entity
Scroll to the website footer. Note the exact company name and the licence number it claims. No entity name is your first red flag.
Go to the regulator, not the broker
Open the regulator's own register in a new tab. Never trust a licence badge or a PDF the broker sends you.
Match every detail
Company name, licence number, website domain and phone number should all match the register entry. One mismatch can mean a clone.
Check the status
Authorised, revoked or expired are very different things. A licence that used to exist protects you from nothing today.
Search the warning lists
Run the name through the FCA Warning List, IOSCO I-SCAN and your local regulator's alerts. Two minutes, and it catches a lot.

ig:
Most bad broker experiences start before the first trade. They start at the deposit.

Here is the 5-minute check we would run on any broker before sending a single dollar: entity, register, match, status, warning lists.

Save this for the next time a broker looks too good.
x:
Five-minute broker check before you deposit:

1. Find the legal entity
2. Open the regulator's register yourself
3. Match name, licence no. and domain
4. Check the licence status
5. Search the warning lists

data.title: Leverage does not make you a better trader. It makes every mistake bigger, and faster.
data.sub: It increases position size, not skill. The same move that doubles a stake can wipe it out.

ig:
Leverage increases the size of your position, not the quality of your decisions.

That is why major regulators cap it for retail traders. Before you use it, work out what a 1% move against you would do to your account.
x:
Leverage does not make you a better trader.

It makes every mistake bigger, and faster.

data.meaning: No regulated broker can promise returns. Markets do not offer guarantees, so whoever is offering one is selling something else.
data.action: Close the chat. Search the name on the regulator's warning list.

ig:
"Risk-free" and "guaranteed" are the two most expensive words in trading.

A regulated broker gives you a risk warning, not a promise. When someone guarantees a monthly return, the product being sold is the promise itself.
x:

data.title: What a strong regulator actually does for you
slides: Segregated client money
Your funds are held separately from the broker's own money, so they are not used to run the business.
Capital requirements
The broker must hold minimum capital, which lowers the risk of sudden collapse.
A complaints route
If the broker will not resolve a dispute, you can escalate to the regulator or an ombudsman.
Compensation, in some places
Schemes such as the FSCS (UK) or Cyprus's ICF may cover eligible clients if a firm fails.
Retail protections
Leverage limits and negative balance protection under rules such as ESMA (EU) and ASIC (Australia).

ig:
A licence is not a stamp. It is a set of obligations a broker must keep.

The strength of those obligations varies hugely by regulator. That is why who regulates your broker matters more than whether it is "regulated" somewhere.
x:
A licence is not a stamp. It is a set of obligations.

Segregated funds, capital rules, complaints routes, compensation schemes and retail protections vary a lot by regulator.

data.definition: The standard unit of price movement in forex. For most pairs it is the fourth decimal place (0.0001).
data.example: EUR/USD 1.1000 → 1.1005 is a 5-pip move. For JPY pairs a pip is the second decimal (0.01).

ig:
Every forex cost and result is measured in pips, so it pays to get this one right.

For most pairs a pip is 0.0001. For JPY pairs it is 0.01.
x:
Pip: the standard unit of forex price movement.

0.0001 for most pairs. 0.01 for JPY pairs.

data.title: 8 signs your 'broker' is not really a broker
slides: They guarantee profits
No regulated broker can promise returns. A guarantee is a sales line, not a product.
An 'account manager' calls daily
Constant calls pushing you to trade or deposit more are a sales operation, not a service.
The bonus has strings
Volume requirements that lock your deposit until you trade a huge amount are a trap.
The licence is not on the register
If the regulator's own site does not list them, the badge on their site means nothing.
They pressure you to top up
"Deposit now to recover your losses" is how small losses become large ones.
Withdrawals stall 'under review'
A real broker pays out in hours to days. Weeks of silence is a warning.
You must pay to withdraw
A 'tax' or 'release fee' paid upfront is the classic last step of a scam.
Crypto-only deposits
Payments that cannot be reversed suit the broker, not you.

ig:
The broker, not the market, is often the real risk.

These eight patterns show up again and again in complaints. One on its own is a reason to slow down. Two or more is a reason to walk away.

Save this and share it with someone who is just starting out.

1. Guaranteed profits
2. Daily sales calls
3. Bonus that locks your deposit
4. Licence not on the register
5. Pressure to top up
6. Withdrawals 'under review'
7. Fees to withdraw
8. Crypto-only deposits

data.title: What a 1% move does at different leverage
slides: The setup
You put $1,000 of margin into a position. The market moves 1% against you.
Position: $10,000. A 1% move = $100. You lose 10% of your margin.
Position: $30,000. A 1% move = $300. You lose 30% of your margin.
Position: $100,000. A 1% move = $1,000. Your margin is gone.
Position: $500,000. A 0.2% move = $1,000. Your margin is gone in a move many currencies make in an ordinary day.

ig:
Run these numbers before you choose a leverage setting.

The same 1% move is a bad day at 1:10 and the end of the account at 1:100. Simplified example — excludes spreads, swaps and fees.
x:
$1,000 margin. Market moves 1% against you.

1:10 → lose $100
1:30 → lose $300
1:100 → lose $1,000

At 1:500, a 0.2% move does the same.

data.title: Clone firms: when scammers copy a real, regulated broker
slides: How it works
Scammers copy a genuine firm's name, licence number and branding, then build a lookalike website.
Why it convinces
You check the register, the name is there, the number matches. It passes a quick check.
Spot the gap
The register lists the real firm's website, email and phone. The clone's contact details will not match.
Contact the firm yourself
Use only the phone number or website shown on the regulator's register, never the one you were sent.
Check the warnings
Regulators such as the FCA (UK) publish clone warnings. Search the firm's name plus 'clone'.

ig:
A real licence number on a fake website is still a fake website.

Clone firms borrow the identity of a genuinely regulated broker. The fix is simple: check the contact details on the register, not just the name.
x:

data.title: The 'online friend' investment scam, step by step
slides: A stranger says hello
A wrong-number text, a dating match or a social media message. Friendly, patient, no rush.
Trust builds over weeks
Daily chats, shared photos, life stories. Money is not mentioned yet.
Then the 'opportunity'
They show you their profits on a trading platform and offer to teach you.
Small wins, bigger deposits
The fake platform shows gains. You may even withdraw a little — that is the hook.
The exit
Big withdrawal requests meet fees, 'taxes' or silence. The platform and the friend disappear.

ig:
The most effective scams are slow.

This pattern can run for weeks before money is mentioned, and the trading platform is usually fake from day one. If someone you have only met online starts teaching you to trade, stop and check the platform independently.

data.title: How much is a pip worth to you?
slides: The rule
Pip value depends on your lot size and the pair. For pairs quoted in USD, it is simple.
1 standard lot of EUR/USD
100,000 units × 0.0001 = about $10 per pip.
1 mini lot of EUR/USD
10,000 units × 0.0001 = about $1 per pip.
1 micro lot of EUR/USD
1,000 units × 0.0001 = about $0.10 per pip.
So a 20-pip stop costs...
About $200 on a standard lot, $20 on a mini, $2 on a micro. Size the trade to the loss you accept.

ig:
Sizing a trade starts with one question: how much is each pip worth to me?

Work it out before you enter, and the stop-loss becomes a number you chose rather than a surprise.
x:
Pip value on EUR/USD:

Standard lot ≈ $10
Mini lot ≈ $1
Micro lot ≈ $0.10

A 20-pip stop is $200, $20 or $2. Size to the loss you accept.

data.title: ECN vs market maker: what is the difference?
slides: Market maker
The broker takes the other side of your trade and sets its own prices. Usually fixed or wider spreads, no commission.
ECN / STP
Your order is passed to outside liquidity providers. Usually raw spreads plus a commission.
The conflict question
A market maker can profit when clients lose. Strong regulation and fair execution policies matter here.
Neither is automatically better
Costs and execution depend on the broker. Check regulation first, then compare total costs.

ig:
ECN or market maker is a business model, not a badge of honesty.

Both can be well run or badly run. Check the licence first, then compare the total cost of the way you trade.

data.title: 6 questions every broker should answer clearly
slides: Which entity will hold my account?
Global brands run several entities. The one you sign with decides your protection.
Who regulates that entity?
Ask for the regulator and licence number, then check it yourself on the register.
Where is client money held?
You want to hear 'segregated accounts' and the name of the bank.
What does a withdrawal cost and how long?
A clear answer is normal. A vague one is not.
Do I have negative balance protection?
